articles.title: A Michigan 5-year-old found his grandmother unconscious, kept his 3-year-old sister safe and ran down a rural road for help; months later, officials honored him for helping save her life
articles.summary: A five-year-old boy in Michigan has been recognised for his quick thinking after his grandmother collapsed during a medical emergency, prompting him to
articles.body: A five-year-old boy in Michigan has been recognised for his quick thinking after his grandmother collapsed during a medical emergency, prompting him to seek help while ensuring his three-year-old sister remained safe. The incident, reported by People and local news outlet WDIV-TV, took place in Cottrellville Township, where the young boy’s actions helped bring emergency assistance to his grandmother, Terri Ketelhut. The children were visiting their grandmother when she suddenly became unwell and fell to the floor. Hudson Tenn, who was five at the time, realised that she was not getting back up. With his younger sister, Harper, beside him, he tried to work out how to get help. Unable to find his grandmother’s car keys, Hudson decided to leave the house and look for someone who could assist. He took Harper with him and headed down a rural road, where the children were spotted by passing neighbours.A quick decision that made a differenceJason Markel and his son, Colton, were travelling along the road when they noticed the two young children. Hudson approached them to ask for help, while making sure Harper stayed safely on the grass beside the road. The pair stopped and brought the children into their truck before calling 911. Hudson then guided them back to the house, helping them locate his grandmother.When Markel reached the residence, he could see Ketelhut lying unconscious inside. However, barking dogs prevented him from immediately entering the property. Emergency responders and deputies from the St. Clair County Sheriff’s Office arrived soon afterwards and began assisting the woman. According to local outlet WDIV-TV, one of the dogs was positioned near Ketelhut, complicating efforts to reach her. Deputies had to move the animal away before emergency medical personnel could provide treatment.Ketelhut was subsequently taken to hospital, where medical examinations determined that dehydration had caused her collapse. The episode came as a shock to the family, as she had not previously experienced a medical emergency of this kind. The timely intervention by the neighbours and emergency services ensured that she received the care she needed.Children recognised for their braveryMonths after the incident, Hudson and Harper were honoured for their actions at a Cottrellville Township board meeting on October 14, 2026. Both children received Citizen Citation Awards in recognition of their role in getting help during the emergency.According to township officials, they are the youngest recipients of the award in St. Clair County’s history. Hudson was particularly praised for recognising that something was wrong, taking the initiative to find assistance and guiding the neighbours back to the house. His decision to keep his younger sister close and out of the roadway also demonstrated remarkable awareness for a child of his age.For the family, the recognition marked a moment of gratitude after an incident that could have ended very differently. Ketelhut expressed appreciation for the people who stopped to help and the deputies who responded to the emergency. What began as a frightening situation at home has since become a story of a young child responding with courage and determination. Hudson could not provide medical care himself, but he understood that his grandmother needed help and took the steps he could to get it.His actions, alongside Harper’s safety-conscious presence and the neighbours’ swift response, helped ensure that an adult medical emergency did not become an even greater tragedy.You use AI every day. articles.title: Joni Mitchell moved from Canada to the United States in the mid-1960s and built much of her career there; 62 years later, at age 82, the legendary singer-songwriter has officially become a US citizen and can now vote
articles.summary: Canadian-born singer-songwriter Joni Mitchell has officially become a United States citizen, marking a significant milestone in a life and career closely
articles.body: Canadian-born singer-songwriter Joni Mitchell has officially become a United States citizen, marking a significant milestone in a life and career closely intertwined with American music. As reported by Billboard and the Los Angeles Times, the 82-year-old musician shared news of her naturalisation on October 13, 2026, more than six decades after first arriving in the country. Mitchell announced the development on social media, posting a photograph of herself holding a small American flag alongside footage from her citizenship ceremony. The announcement brings a new chapter to a journey that began in 1965, when she moved to the United States with her then-husband, musician Chuck Mitchell. Although the singer has not publicly explained what prompted her decision to pursue citizenship, the milestone gives her the right to vote in US elections, provided she meets the applicable registration and voting requirements.From Canada to the heart of American musicBorn Roberta Joan Anderson on November 7, 1943, in Fort Macleod, Alberta, Mitchell grew up in Saskatchewan before beginning her musical journey across the border. Her early travels took her to Detroit and later New York, before she settled in Southern California.Los Angeles became a defining setting in her artistic life. By the late 1960s, Mitchell was closely associated with Laurel Canyon, the hillside neighbourhood that became a gathering place for influential musicians and songwriters of the era. She shared creative connections with artists including David Crosby and Graham Nash, while developing a distinctive musical identity that blended folk, jazz, pop and deeply personal storytelling. Her move to the United States helped place her at the centre of a changing music scene, but her influence would eventually extend far beyond any one city or genre.An enduring legacy in musicAcross a career spanning several decades, Mitchell has earned recognition for her songwriting, unconventional musical arrangements and willingness to explore intimate subjects through her work. Her catalogue includes celebrated songs such as Big Yellow Taxi, Both Sides, Now, River and A Case of You. Her 1971 album Blue remains one of her most acclaimed recordings, widely admired for its emotional candour and sparse, expressive arrangements.Another major release, Court and Spark (1974), brought her considerable commercial success, reaching No. 2 on the Billboard 200 chart. Her song Help Me, from the same album, peaked at No. 7 on the Billboard Hot 100. Mitchell’s contributions have also been recognised through numerous honours, including 11 Grammy Awards. Her influence can be heard across generations of musicians who have drawn inspiration from her lyrical precision, melodic experimentation and refusal to remain within conventional boundaries.A new chapter after decades in the USMitchell’s relationship with American politics has occasionally entered the public conversation. During a 2024 performance at the Hollywood Bowl, she criticised then-presidential candidate Donald Trump and highlighted the limitations of her status as a Canadian citizen when it came to participating in US elections. Her new citizenship marks a change in that position, giving her the opportunity to take part in the country’s electoral process as an eligible voter.For an artist whose work has become deeply embedded in American cultural history, the development is a personal milestone as well as a notable moment in her long relationship with the country. articles.title: Daymond John started FUBU from his mother’s Queens home with a $40 fabric budget and sold $800 of hats in one day; the brand later grew from that tiny start to more than $6 billion in global sales

articles.body: Before Daymond John became a familiar face on Shark Tank, he was a young entrepreneur trying to turn a small idea into a clothing business, working from his mother’s home in Queens, New York. According to ABC News and a 2018 account of his career at RECon, the FUBU co-founder began with just $40 for fabric, eventually building a brand that generated more than $6 billion in global sales. His journey highlights how family support, resourcefulness and an understanding of popular culture helped transform a modest venture into a major name in hip-hop fashion.A small investment that sparked a businessJohn launched FUBU in 1992, drawing on his interest in fashion and the growing influence of hip-hop culture. With limited money available, he bought approximately $40 worth of fabric and used sewing skills taught to him by his mother, Margot John, to make tie-top hats.He took the finished hats to a street corner in Queens and sold the entire batch in a single day, bringing in $800. The sales offered an early indication that there was a market for clothing that reflected the style and identity of young hip-hop fans.Rather than immediately establishing a conventional manufacturing operation, John and his family began building the business from home. Their living room became a makeshift production space, with his mother playing a central role in helping him pursue the venture.FUBU, short for For Us, By Us, was built around clothing designed for a community that John believed was underserved by mainstream fashion brands. Its identity was closely tied to hip-hop, an emerging cultural force that would go on to influence music, entertainment and global streetwear.His mother helped keep the dream aliveMargot John was instrumental in turning the early idea into a business capable of taking larger orders. After the venture struggled to secure conventional financing, she took out a second mortgage on the family home, reportedly releasing around $100,000 in equity to support the company.The financial commitment came after John and his associates faced repeated rejections from banks. ABC News reported in 2016 that 27 lenders had turned them down when they sought funding. His mother also encouraged him to remain persistent while taking responsibility for his ambitions. Her willingness to put the family home at risk demonstrated the confidence she had in his potential, even when outside institutions were reluctant to back the business.John continued working at Red Lobster while developing FUBU, using his earnings to help sustain the venture. The combination of a regular job, family support and an unconventional approach to funding allowed him to continue pursuing growth without the financial backing that many startups seek at the outset.Hip-hop culture helped FUBU find its audienceBuilding the product was only one part of the challenge. John also needed to introduce FUBU to consumers and establish its credibility within the culture that had inspired it. He approached musicians and other emerging cultural figures, encouraging them to wear the brand. One of the most significant connections was with Queens-born rapper LL Cool J, whose association with FUBU helped bring the label to a wider audience.In 1997, LL Cool J wore a FUBU hat in a Gap television commercial and incorporated the brand into a freestyle rap. The appearance became a memorable example of how music, celebrity and fashion could work together to create visibility for a young label. John also pursued opportunities to showcase the clothing at trade events, including a Las Vegas trade show, where he and his team worked to attract buyers and secure orders. As demand grew, the business needed more capital and manufacturing capacity to fulfil its ambitions. A financing opportunity eventually emerged through Samsung Textiles, helping the company move beyond its early limitations. The episode illustrated the importance of persistence and finding unconventional routes when traditional funding options failed.From a homegrown label to a global businessFUBU went on to become one of the defining names associated with the rise of hip-hop-inspired streetwear during the 1990s and early 2000s. Its success demonstrated that a brand rooted in a specific community could reach an international audience by building a clear identity and connecting with its customers. John later expanded his career into entrepreneurship education, writing and television. As an investor on ABC’s Shark Tank, he became known for evaluating businesses and backing entrepreneurs seeking capital and commercial guidance.His experiences also informed his book The Power of Broke, published in 2016, which explores how limited resources can push entrepreneurs to become more inventive and strategic. Rather than treating a lack of money as an automatic barrier, John argues that constraints can encourage founders to make better use of the people, skills and opportunities already available to them.From selling a small batch of hats on a Queens street corner to helping build a multibillion-dollar fashion brand, John’s story reflects the role of cultural insight, persistence and family backing in entrepreneurship. FUBU’s growth was not the result of a single lucky break, but of turning a modest beginning into a business that understood its audience and found ways to reach it.You use AI every day. articles.title: Uttarakhand minister Rekha Arya's husband to woman in explosive audio: 'I'll get her killed, you'll get bail, don't worry'
articles.summary: DEHRADUN: Uttarakhand cabinet minister Rekha Arya has filed a police complaint against her husband, Girdhari Lal Sahu, also known as Pappu Girdhari,
articles.body: DEHRADUN: Uttarakhand cabinet minister Rekha Arya has filed a police complaint against her husband, Girdhari Lal Sahu, also known as Pappu Girdhari, accusing him of physical assault, cheating, forgery and conspiring to kill her.The FIR was registered at Garhi Cantt police station around 7.25pm on Thursday under 13 sections of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), including Section 120-B (criminal conspiracy), Section 323 (voluntarily causing hurt) and Section 420 (cheating). It also invokes three provisions of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989.Arya, the state's women empowerment and child development minister, later shared a video on social media, explaining why she had approached the police. She alleged that the recording contained a conversation in which Sahu discussed a conspiracy to kill her and said she feared for the safety of her minor children.‘Shaken’ by the recordingIn her video statement, Arya said the audio had "shaken" her and "put a question mark on my relationship"."Is this the result one gets for living with truth and honesty?" she asked."After hearing this audio, with pain in my heart, I had to take this decision. I had to file a complaint with the police to protect my children, for the safety of my children," she said.Arya alleged that the conversation indicated a threat to her life. She said she feared that Sahu could commit a serious crime against her or her children.The minister was taken to hospital after reporting that she felt unwell. Further details about her condition were not immediately available.What the audio allegedly revealsThe 8-minute-27-second recording, shared by the minister, purportedly captures Sahu speaking to a woman about bail and the possibility of her going to jail.In the recording, Sahu can allegedly be heard reassuring the woman, calling her "mere babu, mere babu", that he would be there for her and that she would get bail. He then discusses the possibility of her being denied bail and having to go to jail.The woman reportedly asks why she would go to jail and expresses concern that the news would become public and damage her image.Sahu appears to reassure her that nothing would come out.The recording also allegedly contains Sahu assuring the woman that Arya would be dead, along with abusive language.The audio and video were shared on the minister’s social media handles.TOI could not independently verify the veracity of the audio recordings.Allegations of deception and assaultIn her complaint, Arya said she married Sahu in Bareilly, Uttar Pradesh, on July 6, 2004. She alleged that he had represented himself as unmarried despite having a wife and children from an earlier marriage.According to the complaint, she discovered the alleged deception several years later but remained silent for the sake of their children.Arya further alleged that Sahu subsequently became involved with other women. She claimed that he offered written and verbal apologies when confronted but continued the relationships.The complaint alleges that his behaviour became violent when she objected.The FIR states: "upon opposing these relationships, Girdhari Lal Sahu started physically assaulting, abusing, and threatening to kill the applicant."Arya also alleged that Sahu used caste-based slurs against her in front of staff at her official residence. She said the abuse and threats continued, leaving her fearful for her safety and that of her children.Forgery allegations and appeal to womenThe minister also accused Sahu of forging her signature and preparing fabricated documents to show that she had retired as a director of companies with which she was associated. She alleged that she had neither signed the documents nor submitted any resignation.In her video statement, Arya urged women not to remain silent in the face of domestic abuse, regardless of their social or public standing."Whether a woman is ordinary or prominent, she must not bear domestic atrocities. She must not bear them; she must speak out," she said.Arya added that she had always discharged her duties "with the Constitution as witness" and would continue to do so. She also said her maternal family had consistently supported her."Even in this pain, I have not forgotten my duty... For anything further, I am speechless," she said.Stay updated with the latest Dehradun news. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: A Scottish Labrador once trained for mountain rescue learned to sniff out an invasive marine creature called ‘sea vomit’; after finding hundreds of colonies, Sgiath was named Animal of the Year
articles.summary: A black Labrador from the Scottish Highlands has found an unusual new calling beneath the waves, and it has earned her international recognition.
articles.body: A black Labrador from the Scottish Highlands has found an unusual new calling beneath the waves, and it has earned her international recognition. Sgiath, a six-year-old dog once trained for mountain rescue, has become the first dog in the world trained to detect an invasive marine organism nicknamed “sea vomit”. Her remarkable ability to locate the creature, even when it is concealed among other marine life, has helped her win the Animal of the Year award from the International Fund for Animal Welfare (IFAW).The award recognises more than an extraordinary canine skill. It highlights a creative approach to marine conservation, where a dog’s powerful sense of smell could help scientists identify a damaging invasive species before it spreads further. Sgiath’s work offers conservationists another way to monitor vulnerable coastal environments and protect native marine life.From mountain rescue missions to an unexpected underwater missionSgiath’s career took a surprising turn when her handler, marine ecologist Dr Texa Sim, began exploring whether a dog could help address a problem facing Scotland’s west coast. Sim, originally from Glasgow and now based near Glencoe, was working on a native oyster restoration project when she became increasingly concerned about invasive marine species. One species in particular caught her attention: Didemnum vexillum, commonly called carpet sea squirt and sometimes referred to as “sea vomit”. The organism can spread across harbours, oyster farms and other marine structures, forming dense colonies that smother native species and disrupt local ecosystems.Detecting it is not always straightforward. Identification can require specialist laboratory work and DNA testing, making early detection challenging for people managing marine sites. Sim wondered whether a dog’s exceptional sense of smell could offer a faster and more practical way to locate the organism. The idea was experimental. Dogs are widely known for detecting scents in search-and-rescue operations, but using one to identify a marine organism presented a different challenge. Sim began training Sgiath to recognise the target species among a range of similar smells.The early results surprised her. “The first time I asked her to identify the target species among lots of similar scents, she went straight to it,” Sim recalled. “That was the moment I thought: maybe this is actually going to work.” Sgiath’s performance helped turn an uncertain experiment into a promising conservation project. According to Sim, the work has resulted in the detection of hundreds of colonies, demonstrating how scent detection could complement existing monitoring methods.How one dog could help protect marine ecosystemsCarpet sea squirt is a concern because it can establish itself quickly and spread over surfaces in coastal waters. Once dense colonies take hold, they can smother other organisms and create difficulties for marine habitats and industries such as oyster farming. Finding an invasive species early gives conservationists a better opportunity to assess the problem and decide how to respond. Sgiath’s ability to identify its scent could help direct attention to areas that need closer examination, potentially reducing the time and effort required to locate colonies.Sim has been candid about the experimental nature of the work. She did not know at the outset whether the training would succeed, as the use of dogs to detect this kind of marine organism had not been widely explored. “When I first started this project, I genuinely didn’t know whether it would work,” she said. “No one had really explored whether dogs could help tackle this problem in the marine environment. It began as a proof-of-concept project and has exceeded every expectation I had.”The approach is not intended to replace scientific testing or eliminate the threat posed by invasive species. Instead, it could provide an additional tool for researchers and site managers, helping them locate suspected colonies for further investigation. Climate change makes such efforts increasingly relevant. Warmer seas can create more favourable conditions for some invasive marine organisms to spread into new areas. Recent summer heatwaves have also raised concerns about the effects of elevated sea temperatures on marine ecosystems.“We’re not going to solve the problem entirely with dogs,” Sim said. “But they give us another tool. If we can identify the species earlier and more efficiently, it gives conservationists and site managers a much better chance of responding before the problem gets out of hand.”A global award for a four-legged conservation pioneerSgiath received IFAW’s Animal of the Year award at a ceremony in London on Thursday. The annual honour recognises animals whose actions have made an extraordinary contribution, and the charity said Sgiath’s work stood out for opening up a new possibility in conservation science. Sharon Livermore, IFAW’s director of marine conservation, praised the dog’s unusual contribution and the potential of the project.“Every year, the Animal of the Year award celebrates animals doing extraordinary things, but Sgiath’s story is like nothing we’ve seen before,” Livermore said. She added that the dog’s work demonstrated how dogs could contribute to conservation science in new ways. Livermore also pointed to warmer seas and the increased urgency of detecting invasive species early. She noted that Sgiath’s previous mountain rescue abilities would already have made her worthy of recognition, but her pioneering marine detection work had added another dimension to her contribution.For Sgiath, the journey from mountain rescue training to marine conservation is a reminder that an animal’s abilities can find unexpected uses. For scientists, her success offers a practical question worth pursuing: could scent-trained dogs help spot other invasive species before they become harder to control? Dogs alone will not solve the challenges facing the world’s oceans. But Sgiath has shown that an extraordinary nose, paired with careful scientific training, can become a valuable ally in the effort to protect marine life.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: India and Russia begin naval wargame INDRA  in Russian waters
articles.summary: India and Russia are conducting the 2026 edition of Exercise INDRA, their bilateral naval exercise, with the Indian Navy's indigenously built stealth
articles.body: India and Russia are conducting the 2026 edition of Exercise INDRA, their bilateral naval exercise, with the Indian Navy's indigenously built stealth frigate INS Sahyadri arriving at Vladivostok on October 10. The exercise runs from October 13 to 18 and brings personnel from the Indian Navy and the Russian Navy together for harbour-based engagements and coordinated activities at sea. The wargame is intended to improve mutual understanding, operational coordination and interoperability, and the programme includes professional interactions, maritime evolutions and social and cultural exchanges. The ministry has not detailed the sea-phase drills in its arrival announcement.The deployment forms part of India's wider maritime engagement under its MAHASAGAR vision, Mutual and Holistic Advancement for Security and Growth Across Regions. The ministry has also linked the visit to the momentum from the 23rd India-Russia Annual Summit, held on December 4 and 5, 2025.INS Sahyadri is the third ship of the Shivalik-class guided-missile stealth frigates. It was designed and built in India, commissioned in 2012. It carries weapons and sensors to counter threats in the air, on the surface and underwater. The frigate took part in the Japan-India Maritime Exercise in October 2025, which involved anti-submarine warfare and missile-defence drills and has exercised with other navies, including France's.INDRA began in 2003 as a bilateral naval exercise, with the name combining those of the two countries. The first edition was held in two phases off India's western and eastern coasts in May and June 2003. The framework later grew to include the Army and Air Force. In October 2017, the two countries held their first joint tri-service INDRA in Russia, with more than 900 Indian and over 1,000 Russian personnel covering counter-terrorism, joint command structures, naval force protection and air defence. The second tri-service edition was held in India in December 2019, at Babina, Pune and Goa, focusing on counter-terrorism and counter-insurgency under a United Nations mandate.The naval exercise has continued separately. The 14th edition was held from March 28 to April 2, 2025, off Chennai and in the Bay of Bengal, with the Indian ships Rana and Kuthar and a P-8I maritime patrol aircraft taking part alongside the Russian vessels Pechanga, Rezkiy and Aldar Tsydenzhapov. The sea phase included tactical manoeuvres, live weapon firings, anti-air operations, underway replenishment and helicopter cross-deck landings. The 2026 edition moves the exercise to Russian waters, with Vladivostok as the host port.INDRA is one part of a wider defence relationship covering training, equipment supplies, licensed production, joint research and defence-industrial cooperation, coordinated through the India-Russia Inter-Governmental Commission on Military and Military Technical Cooperation. The BrahMos missile was jointly developed by the two countries, HAL builds the Su-30MKI under licence, and T-90S tanks are produced in India. The AK-203 rifle is being made through the Indo-Russia Rifles Private Limited joint venture, and India has bought the S-400 air defence system. On the naval side, Russia was involved in transferring and refurbishing INS Vikramaditya, and the Russian-built frigates INS Tushil and INS Tamal were commissioned in December 2024 and July 2025.

articles.title: An 84-year-old Australian pensioner left his home to an online wife he never met; a court ruled she did not exist and awarded his estate to his daughter
articles.summary: Clifford Stanley Perrin died in Maryborough Hospital on Christmas Eve 2025, aged 84 and divorced.
articles.body: Clifford Stanley Perrin died in Maryborough Hospital on Christmas Eve 2025, aged 84 and divorced. He had been the victim of a scam that depleted his finances, leaving his estate with one asset: a small property in Hervey Bay, which was subject to a reverse mortgage. According to the Supreme Court of Queensland judgment in the Will of Clifford Stanley Perrin [2026] QSC 247, his handmade will named the scammer, whose purported name was Stella Helena Perrin, as executor and beneficiary. On 24 September 2026, Treston J found that she did not exist and that her appointment and the gift to her failed.How did a fake online lover target an Australian pensioner’s homeMr Perrin was born on 24 February 1941 and did not finish high school, but worked in a variety of occupations during his working life. His father died in about 1986 and his mother in 2004, and in the years before her death he was her full-time carer. In 2005 he retired to a modest home in Point Vernon, Hervey Bay, where he lived until he went into hospital before his death. He was briefly married between April 1971 and June 1976, and the marriage ended in divorce.The judgment records that his only daughter was born shortly after the marriage in 1971. While she was growing up she was told her father was deceased, and she learned otherwise in her twenties. Around 2010, a DNA test showed a 99.99 per cent chance that Mr Perrin was her father. The court noted that the relationship was "not a particularly close one" and that, after about 2019, he appears to have stopped contacting her entirely. In about 2012, he befriended a local bus driver, Mr Kim, who began picking him up two or three times a week. Mr Kim observed that Mr Perrin was a lonely man who lived alone and did not appear to have a regular circle of friends.How did a fake online wife convince a pensioner he was married to herUnknown to both his daughter and Mr Kim, Mr Perrin had one other friend, a woman called Stella Helena Bennett. Records obtained after his death indicate that he met her over the internet in about 2012. She told him she was born in 1976, a former fashion model from an upper middle-class family in New York, who lived in the town of Massena. At that time, Mr Perrin was a 71-year-old pensioner with significantly impaired vision who could no longer drive. According to the court, he had never travelled to New York and had never met Stella. Even so, on 25 April 2013 he considered that he had married her. In an email to a friend on 6 May 2013, headed "Take a seat before you read this, Pete", he described Stella as his wife and said she was coming to live in Point Vernon.Stella told him they had been married by proxy and later sent him a copy of a marriage certificate, which the court found to be a forgery. Around the time they connected online, she also said she had received a large inheritance from her father, held in New York by a Zimbabwe-based company, which she could not access until tax was paid. The judgment records that she sought his financial assistance and identity information to pay the Internal Revenue Service, and promised to move to Hervey Bay with the balance of the funds. In 2014, she told him she had moved to Kuala Lumpur and become a Malaysian citizen. She later said Malaysian taxes were blocking the inheritance and gave him an "inheritance tax bond disclosure" and a letter purportedly from "MPI Generali Insurans Bhd". The court found both documents were false, and stressed that there was no suggestion the legitimate company had any part in producing them.How did a pensioner’s fake online wife obtain his money and inheritanceStella extracted various funds from Mr Perrin over time. The evidence shows she asked him to transfer money to accounts in other people's names, send Bitcoin, send iTunes Gift Cards and Steam Wallet Cards, provide cash to unspecified third parties, and mail new SIM cards or iPhones to her. At different times she also obtained his credit card information, bank details, myGov account details and identity documents. In May 2024 his own bank blocked a transfer, and a bank employee told him the receiving account was associated with a scam. The court found that Mr Perrin suggested Stella simply prove her identity, but that she instead suggested he tell the bank he was sending money to a family member who needed medical help.The will is dated 3 May 2024, although the evidence suggests it may have been executed on 4 May 2024. It was witnessed in the presence of two justices of the peace. The court described it as a handmade document in two parts. Part A revokes earlier wills and appoints Stella, "my wife", as executor and trustee, recording that she lived in Kuala Lumpur. It also bequeaths the bulk of the estate to her. A further dot point provides that if Stella should "pass away before my death", the entire estate goes to his daughter. The court found that Mr Perrin was not shown to lack testamentary capacity and that the will was duly executed. It found no earlier will.How did a court expose an Australian pensioner’s fake online wifeThe court gave nine reasons for finding that Stella was "either not a real person or does not exist at all". They included the improbable nature of the supposed match, and the marriage certificate, which bore no seal, named "Fresno County of New York" although Fresno County is in California, referred to "New York State Republic", and misspelt the bride's name. The applicant's solicitors also confirmed with the Massena Town Hall that no such marriage certificate was registered. The judge accepted evidence that, after Mr Perrin's death, Stella refused to prove her identity when asked, asked for money first, and then deleted the message exchange. The court also found that during his lifetime she suggested he gift money immediately rather than wait to die, and that she repeatedly pressed him to take out a reverse mortgage on his property. Applying the Briginshaw standard, the judge concluded that the evidence strongly supported the inference that Stella had perpetrated a romance scam.On the legal question, Treston J applied the rule in Jones v Westcomb, concluding that Mr Perrin must have intended the gift over to his daughter to operate if Stella never existed. The judge relied on the wording of the clause, which was functionally the same as in Re the Will of William Ian Southey [2025] VSC 801, and on emails in which Mr Perrin recorded suspicions of Stella in January 2015 and again in August 2024. The judge said that, had the rule not applied, the parts of the will affected by his false assumption about her character or identity would have been severed, following Kennell v Abbott. The court ordered that the will be pronounced in solemn form of law and declared that the applicant, Tanya Maree Stankovich, was entitled to probate as executor and to the residue as sole beneficiary. It also ordered that costs be paid out of the estate on the indemnity basis.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
